goal: Bend light at both surfaces, with any object, camera and scene, as a drop-in GLSL MAT.
alternatives: Core single-surface offset (refract once, slide by Thickness); ray tracing or ray marching the object (needs the object as an SDF or a BVH); Wyman-style two-surface image-space refraction.
evidence: References 1 and 4 show light leaving through a second, differently tilted surface (flipped, doubled images and bright trapped bands). The core's limits section names exit refraction and total internal reflection as missing. Heckel's backside section and the Wyman 2005 lineage give a two-pass image-space method that keeps the material universal.
choice: Per pixel and per spectrum slice: refract in (enterGlass), find the exit point and the far side's normal, refract out (leaveGlass: Snell's law plus Fresnel), continue Scene depth further and read the Refraction TOP at the projected point.
consequence: A new control, Scene depth, says how far behind the glass the scene sits. A slab now gives zero net deviation (tested). Still screen-space: only what the Refraction TOP shows can appear through the glass.
status: implemented; preview tests slab_zero_net_deviation and ior1_invisible_* pass

goal: Store what the exit needs from the back-face pass: the far side's normal and its distance.
alternatives: (a) Multiple render targets: GLSL MAT writes fragColor[TD_NUM_COLOR_BUFFERS], Render TOP # of Color Buffers = 2 (or 3, keeping the core's back colour), a Render Select TOP (colorbufindex) per buffer. (b) Pack into one RGBA float target: rgb = outward normal, alpha = eye distance. (c) Depth TOP for distance plus a colour pass for normals.
evidence: Write a GLSL MAT (oldid 38399): TD_NUM_COLOR_BUFFERS is set from the render settings and writing beyond the buffers provided can corrupt or crash the GPU, so one shader shared by a 1-buffer render (the glass) and a 2-buffer render (the back pass) would need conditional code per buffer count. The page shows the output array declared two different ways. Render Select TOP's page dates from 2021 (oldid 23988) and does not state the index base. A float target holds signed normals and distances above 1 without encoding. The exit needs no back-face colour: inner reflections are computed in the front pass.
choice: (b): one RGBA 32-bit float target, one colour buffer, no Render Select TOP. rgb = world-space outward normal (signed, unencoded), alpha = minus the eye distance, so glass is alpha < 0 and any non-negative background reads as empty. Read with texelFetch and validity-weighted bilinear weights, so no texture filtering of 32-bit floats is needed.
consequence: The most portable choice: the same shader file serves both passes with a uniform switch, and the back pass needs no multi-buffer support. Cost: the core's back-face colour (Heckel's shaded backside) is not stored; 16 bytes per pixel (about 15 MB at 1280x720). 32-bit floats keep distance precision at large scene scales (16-bit floats step by 0.0625 units at distance 100). Independent review (T5): the Render TOP's background colour is combined with the Camera COMP's, so a camera background with non-zero alpha would have read as glass under the first encoding (alpha = distance, 0 = empty); negating the distance removes that dependence (preview test backface_background_reads_as_empty). Under ACEScg TouchDesigner forces TOPs to 16-bit float, which this choice cannot prevent; documented.
status: implemented; unit test test_backface_pass_is_a_float_data_target; preview test backface_background_reads_as_empty; native check pending

goal: Find the exit point accurately when the back-face pass is on.
alternatives: Use the view-ray thickness as the path (core); Wyman's blend of view-ray and normal-direction distances (needs a precomputed distance along the normal); march the refracted ray against the stored distances.
evidence: The core's view-ray thickness is exact only at IOR 1. A refracted ray reaches the far side somewhere else on screen.
choice: Start with the longer of the view-ray thickness and the ball guess's path (the view-ray thickness shrinks to 0 at the silhouette), then up to four times: project the guess to the screen, read the far side's eye distance there, and move the guess along the ray by the difference divided by how fast the eye distance grows along the ray (clamped). Stop early once a step is tiny. A fixed maximum count.
consequence: The path inside a unit sphere matches the exact refracted chord within 3/255 at IOR 1 and 1.5, out to 0.94 of the sphere's screen radius (preview test). Independent review (M3): the first version (two corrections from the view-ray thickness) reported total reflection on 2,408 of 3,288 sphere pixels between 128 and 131 px of a 133 px radius, where the exact share is at most 0.51; with this start and four corrections, 0. Within about 2 px of the silhouette 201 pixels can still read as trapped (exact share up to 0.94). The far side seen is the nearest back face only.
status: implemented; preview tests backpass_path_matches_sphere_chord, fallback_ball_matches_measured_on_sphere, ball_never_traps_any_wavelength pass

goal: Never break without the back-face pass (universality first).
alternatives: Fall back to the core's single surface; assume a fixed exit normal (for example the mirrored view direction); fit a local shape. A ball alone: its exit normal does not depend on its size, so even a very thin ball bends light like a lens, which is wrong for flat sheets.
evidence: A ball of diameter Thickness that touches the pixel with the same normal has a closed-form exit: path = Thickness cos(a), exit normal = n + 2 cos(a) ray, always unit length and finite. It is exact for a ball. In a ball the exit angle equals the entry angle, so it can never trap light, at any wavelength, provided each wavelength uses its own exit normal (see the dispersion decision); flattened or twisted shapes (reference 1) do trap light.
choice: estimateExit(): the ball, blended by Exit tilt (-1..1). Toward 1: the near normal mirrored through the view direction (a steeper far wall that can trap light at rims). Toward -1: the negated near normal (a far wall parallel to the near one: a flat sheet of thickness Thickness, zero net bend), and the path blends from the ball's Thickness x cos(a) to the sheet's Thickness / cos(a). Control default 0.45, the default preset Spectral Prism's value. Measured on the demo torus (preview, Spectral Prism, tir stage): the back-face pass fully traps 17% of glass pixels; the ball guess traps 20% at Exit tilt 0.3 and 29% at 0.45. So 0.3, which the six core looks keep, is the closer match, and 0.45 is a look choice with wider trapped bands (reference 1); the original reason for 0.45 was not recorded. Found in self-review: without the -1 side, thin flat glass and open surfaces would always magnify.
consequence: Finite everywhere (200 extreme renders read back as 32-bit floats, no NaN or infinity). Exact on a sphere at Exit tilt 0 (within 1/255 of the measured exit, out to 0.97 of its radius) and on a slab at Exit tilt -1 (zero deviation; lookups within 0.04 px of the measured image once Thickness is the slab's thickness). On other shapes it is an estimate. With the back-face pass on, it remains the fallback wherever the pass has no data (mainly near silhouettes), so Exit tilt still matters there. Independent review (M5, T9): the docs had said the default was 0.3 and that Exit tilt had no effect with the pass on; corrected. Independent review (M9): the sheet's path had used the ball's Thickness x cos(a), under-shifting by up to 1.8x at grazing angles; fixed.
status: implemented; preview tests fallback_without_backpass_stays_finite, fallback_ball_matches_measured_on_sphere, slab_zero_net_deviation, flat_guess_matches_measured_slab pass

goal: Total internal reflection that appears exactly past the critical angle, with no jump in the image.
alternatives: A hard switch at the critical angle; Schlick's approximation (needs the transmitted angle inside glass and is inexact near the critical angle); the full Fresnel equations.
evidence: The brief requires TIR beyond the critical angle and not below it, and a continuous look. The Fresnel share rises smoothly to 1 as the angle nears the critical angle.
choice: leaveGlass() returns the outgoing direction and the exact unpolarised Fresnel share; past the critical angle the share is 1. The share splits each slice between the scene through the exit and the bounce.
consequence: Matches Fresnel within 3/255 below the critical angle (for the exact ray through the pixel) and is total beyond it; monotonic in IOR. Near the critical angle the share is very sensitive to angle: 0.03 degrees changed the expected value by 7/255 in the first test run, which is why the test traces the exact pixel ray.
status: implemented; preview tests tir_beyond_critical_angle_only and tir_area_below_and_beyond pass

goal: Show where trapped light goes, cheaply.
alternatives: Trace several bounces (unbounded cost); look up only the environment; one bounce with a scene lookup.
evidence: First previews looked up only the environment: trapped bands read dark because the studio is mostly dark, unlike the bright bands in reference 1. After one mirror bounce most rays head sideways, toward the scene behind.
choice: bounceLight(): one mirror reflection off the far wall, no second exit. Heading away or sideways from the camera it reads the Refraction TOP (a mirrored copy of the scene); heading back toward the camera it reads the environment; smoothstep blend between. Inner reflection scales it; the bounced light is tinted over twice the path.
consequence: Bright, mirrored bands where light is trapped (Trapped Light preset). It is an approximation: the second exit's refraction and further bounces are ignored.
status: implemented

goal: Stronger, correctly ordered rainbow through both surfaces.
alternatives: Core's linear IOR spread per slice; Heckel's per-channel IORs; a Cauchy-shaped spread.
evidence: Real glass follows Cauchy's law closely in the visible range: the blue-violet end spreads more than the red end. Two surfaces roughly double the angular split of one.
choice: sliceIor(): 680 nm (red) to 400 nm (violet), n = Ior + 0.3 x Dispersion x curve, where the curve is (1/wavelength^2 - 1/530^2) normalised to span 1 (red -0.34, violet +0.66), so 530 nm keeps the Ior value. Same Dispersion scale as the core (0.3 IOR span at 1). The exit point and path are traced once with the 530 nm IOR and shared by all slices. Each slice refracts with its own IOR at both surfaces and uses its own far-side normal (sliceExitNormal): the ball formula for its own ray, or, with the back-face pass, a second reading of the pass where that slice arrives (path scaled by the ball's chord ratio, exact for a ball and irrelevant for a flat far side). The diagnostic stages show 680, 530 and 400 nm.
consequence: Through a 45-degree prism the deviations of red, 530 nm and violet match Snell's law within 2/255 of 90 degrees (18.7, 21.9, 28.9 degrees at IOR 1.3, Dispersion 0.3); in the image itself each colour channel matches an independent 16-slice trace within 0.0001. Independent review (M2): with one shared exit normal, violet was falsely trapped on 20,952 of 55,606 pixels of a sphere at Dispersion 1 (16,313 on the torus), contradicting 'a ball never traps light'; now 0 without the pass and 0 inside 0.97 of the radius with it. Cost: with the back-face pass and Dispersion above 0, one extra bilinear read (4 texel fetches) per slice. Sharing one exit point still misses the small spatial spread of the slices inside the glass.
status: implemented; preview tests dispersion_violet_deviates_more, rainbow_in_the_image_follows_snell, ball_never_traps_any_wavelength pass

goal: An optional inner glow where the glass focuses light, without grain.
alternatives: Heckel's derivative area ratio (dFdx/dFdy of positions before and after refraction) in the material; a separate light-space caustics pass; a closed-form ball-lens estimate.
evidence: Screen derivatives are constant over 2x2 pixel quads and per triangle for interpolated normals, which would show blocks or facets on the demo mesh. Heckel's caustics demo also smooths with per-pixel random noise, which the brief rules out. A ball lens has a closed-form focal spot: angular radius |2 - n| / n on the far wall.
choice: causticGlow(): a soft spot around the far-wall direction facing away from the light, radius max(|2 - n| / n, 0.1) x Caustic spread, brightness (1/9) / radius^2 capped at 4 (Heckel's area ratio in closed form). Evaluated per slice, so violet focuses sooner. Caustic spread widens without dimming.
consequence: Continuous and cheap. With the default light in front of the object the spot sits near the lower-right rim; a light behind the object focuses onto the near wall, which this model does not draw. Not a light simulation.
status: implemented; look only (no physical test)

goal: Keep every projected lookup meaningful and smooth, whatever Scene depth and camera distance (independent review T1).
alternatives: Bounded screen offsets as in Heckel's article (uv + refractVec.xy x power, refraction article lines 430-432) and the core study; cap the travel along each ray; blend to the environment as the point nears the camera; clamp in clip space; derive the mip level from screen derivatives of the lookup.
evidence: Preview, instrumented copy (smallest clip w over all projectOffset calls): Spectral Prism on the demo torus put 8% of glass pixels' lookups behind the camera at Scene depth 10 and 28% at 20; with the camera 3 units away, 0.9-2.9% already at Scene depth 5 (inside the slider range). Clamping alone removed every behind-camera lookup but left the image grainy (mean absolute Laplacian inside the glass 53 at Scene depth 2.2, 127 at 20): the larger cause is minification, where neighbouring pixels read unrelated texels at a fixed mip level.
choice: projectOffset(): if the projected point is less than half as far from the camera (clip w) as its reference point, move it along the line toward the reference point until it is; exact and unchanged otherwise, continuous at the switch, perspective only (orthographic w is constant). footprintLod(): each scene and bounce lookup reads at least the mip level its own footprint needs (screen derivatives of the unfolded coordinate), combined with the frost level by max. Derivatives are taken where every pixel runs the same code: the bounce coordinate is computed for every slice when Inner reflection is above 0, not only for trapped ones. The projected 3D lookup itself is kept (it is the study's two-surface model).
consequence: No lookup closer than half the surface's distance for Scene depth up to 50 and the camera 1.8 to 5 units away (instrumented preview test). The Laplacian ratio from Scene depth 2.2 to 20 fell from 2.4 to 1.3 (Spectral Prism) and from 2.5 to 1.5 (Trapped Light). Strongly shrunk views now read as a blurred average instead of grain, which also softens the default look slightly near the rims (captures re-rendered). README and tutorial now call Scene depth a lens strength, not the literal background distance. Family sync: footprintLod() as described here (the full footprint, measured along its longer axis) was compared with a 4 x 4 supersampled render (round-2 B7 method) and measured worse; it now starts 2 levels lower (see the footprint decision below), and large_scene_depth_stays_smooth compares with a supersampled render instead of a fixed ratio.
status: implemented; preview tests lookups_stay_in_front_of_camera, large_scene_depth_stays_smooth pass

goal: Bend the right way whatever the build's screen convention, and make Flip V a complete escape hatch (independent review T7, M6).
alternatives: Trust that the projection's y matches screen V (pending native check only); take the vertical sign from view space; measure it per pixel.
evidence: Every offset goes through uTDMats[].proj in clip space; the docs describe proj only as 'Z range [0,1], Vulkan style'. In a preview emulation of a build whose screen y runs opposite to the projection's y, IOR 1 still matched (zero offsets) but bent images differed from the mirrored reference on about 90,000 pixels by up to 252/255, and Flip V could not fix it because it flipped only the base UV.
choice: At the top of main(), the sign of dFdx and dFdy of the pixel's own projected position gives screenSign (+1 or -1 per axis; the magnitude is 2/width by construction, so only the sign is used). projectOffset() and the flat-image reflection multiply their offsets by it. Flip V flips the base UV and screenSign.y together.
consequence: In the emulated flipped build every prism lookup lands on the mirror of its normal position (0 px error); with an upside-down Refraction TOP and back-face pass, Flip V restores the normal render exactly. The whole default image differs at 1,943 pixels by more than 8/255, where the footprint mip level changes inside a 2 x 2 pixel block (derivatives come from the other row). Quad Reproject cameras are untested. The real TouchDesigner convention is still a native check.
status: implemented; preview tests bends_follow_screen_orientation, flip_v_corrects_upside_down_inputs pass; native check pending; family sync: the derivative measurement was replaced by a comparison with the raster position, with derivatives kept only as the tie-break on the centre lines of odd-sized renders (see C6 below)

goal: Family sync R1: wobble and film drift that never jumps when the speed changes or a morph runs, after any uptime.
alternatives: uWobble.w = absTime.seconds (or Fixed time) multiplied by the morphed Wobble speed in the shader (6a58487); fold absolute time; the core's integrated clock (presets.advance(), phase(), spin()).
evidence: 6a58487 bound uWobble.w to absTime.seconds and computed t = uWobble.w x uWobble.z in wobbleNormal() and filmThickness() (liquid_prism.frag lines 203 and 231). The core measured the defect for the same code: one frame of a 100-frame morph changed the image by up to 226/255 after 1 hour. Unit test here: with the clock at 3600 s, every frame of a 100-frame Spectral Prism to Lavender Prism morph and a fast Wobble speed drag moves the phase by exactly rate x speed x frame time (the 6a58487 recipe has no phase(), so the test errors).

goal: Family sync R5: shader hygiene from the core's round 2, without changing the two-surface optics.
alternatives: Keep the 6a58487 code; port the core's fixes one by one.
evidence: 6a58487: reversed smoothstep(0.0, -0.7, el) in the studio (line 486) and env.frag, and smoothstep(px, -px, d) in backdrop.frag (undefined in GLSL; Metal is the target); an absolute 1e-12 degeneracy test for faceted normals (a mesh without normals built at 1/20 size fell back to facing the camera); TDDeformNorm() applied to a possibly zero normal; the normal laid back toward the camera before the wobble, so ripples could tilt it away again (at IOR 1 that mirrors the view); the wobble slope divided by the Geometry COMP's scale; atan(0, 0) at the poles; unguarded light and half vectors; f0 through pow(). Verifier V3 (after the sync): TDCheckDiscard() still sat right after dPdx and dPdy, before throughGlass(), whose footprintLod() takes dFdx and dFdy of every slice's lookup. Derivative's Write a GLSL MAT (oldid 38399): TDCheckDiscard 'is used in things such as order-indepdendent transparency and dual-paraboloid rendering', so with Order Independent Transparency (which the README recommends for Opacity below 1) a neighbour can be discarded before those derivatives, and GLSL leaves them undefined. The same page says 'For best performance call it at the start of the pixel shader'.
choice: Ordered smoothstep edges in all three shaders (backdrop.frag is now the core's file); dFdx/dFdy of the position at the top of main() with a relative test (facetedNormal()); the vertex stage decides a zero normal before TDDeformNorm; faceCamera() after the wobble on the front pass and its mirror faceAway() on the back-face pass; wobble slope x the cube root of |det(world)|; azimuth(); safeNormalize() for light, half, eye, forward and the exit march direction; f0 = r0 x r0. The per-slice IOR clamp at 1 was already there (sliceIor(), max(..., 1.0)). Verifier V3: TDCheckDiscard() now follows the last derivative in each pass: in the back-face pass at the start of its branch (its derivatives are all at the top of main()), in the glass pass right after throughGlass(). goal: Family sync C6: screen orientation measured per pixel (originated here).

The core measured 2 to 5 wrong pixels per preset on its knot, up to 50/255 off. Both need no branch; the comparison needs no derivatives at all. Verifier round: (V1) the flat-image reflection offsets by rv.xy, a camera-space direction, not a difference of projected points, so the projection's own sign does not cancel there. With a mirrored projection (preview option projFlipY: uTDMats.proj with a negative y scale), its vertical sign agreed with projectOffset()'s camera-up direction on 0 of 98,796 glass pixels, with and without a flipped raster (98,796 of 98,796 with a normal projection). (V2) At an odd render size one pixel row and one column sit exactly on the centre lines, where ndc and raster are both 0; the tie rule (+1) then got the whole centre row wrong in a flipped raster: 1,524 (torus) and 1,548 (knot) pixels at 481 x 271, all on the centre row. The sign of the ndc derivative fixes most of them but was itself wrong on 1 centre-line pixel per knot render (a nearly edge-on triangle: 1/w changes 12.5% to the next pixel, and the extrapolated neighbour lands 2 pixels off). Over 192 renders at 481 x 271 (4 meshes, 48 poses): tie rule alone 0 wrong (normal raster) and 26,268 (flipped); derivative alone 1 and 1; derivative trusted only where 1/w changes by less than 10% to the next pixel 0 and 12 (of 48,467 centre-line pixels).
choice: Measured better, so this study adopts the core's form for its own mechanism: screenSign() compares ndc with 2 x gl_FragCoord / viewport - 1 per axis and applies to every projectOffset(); Flip V flips the base UV and the vertical sign together, as before. projectOffset() needs no projection-sign factor, because its offsets are differences of projected points. The flat-image reflection does (verifier V1): its offset is a camera-space direction, so it uses cam.viewSign = screenSign x the signs of proj[0][0] and proj[1][1], as the core's screenSign() does; the environment lookup in bounceLight() too. On the centre line of an odd-sized render (verifier V2) the sign of the projected position's screen derivative decides, taken at the top of main() in uniform control flow, and only where the surface is not nearly edge-on (1/w changes by less than 10% to the next pixel); elsewhere the tie gives +1.
consequence: 0 wrong pixels in 96 renders (screen_orientation_has_no_wrong_pixels: 12 presets x torus and knot x normal and flipped raster, at 960 x 540 and at 481 x 271; the pre-fix shader had 1,524 and 1,548 at 481 x 271). mirrored_projection_keeps_offsets_the_right_way: with a mirrored projection, upright or upside down, prism lookups land within 0 pixels and flat-image reflection lookups within 0.31 pixel of the normal build (pre-fix: up to 324 pixels off on 98,546 of 98,796 pixels). Known limit: in a build whose raster is flipped, a centre-line pixel of an odd-sized render on a nearly edge-on surface keeps +1 (12 of 48,467 centre-line pixels in the survey); the core uses the plain tie rule, so this is a family-wide point to raise there. No capture changed (all 52 re-rendered: 0/255). Native orientation pending.
